item.title: 'The Quad is not an anti-China coalition' – The US should walk the talk: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02 00:07:00
Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT The Quad's nature should not be determined by how US officials describe it, but by what it actually does. If it uses supply chain security as a pretext to exclude Chinese industries and impose technological restrictions on China, no amount of diplomatic rhetoric can disguise its true nature as a tool of containment against China. On Saturday, the US-Japan-India-Australia (Quad) foreign ministers' meeting issued a joint statement expressing concerns over so-called "economic coercion," "arbitrary export restrictions" and "overcapacity." Although the statement did not name China, its references clearly pointed to it. Interestingly, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that the Quad was not an "anti-China alliance" and was not aimed at any country. We are willing to take Rubio at his word, but more importantly, hope Washington will back its words with actions. The Quad's nature should not be determined by how US officials describe it, but by what it actually does. If its cooperation aims to maintain regional stability and promote industrial development, there is nothing wrong with that. But if it uses supply chain security as a pretext to exclude Chinese industries and impose technological restrictions on China, no amount of diplomatic rhetoric can disguise its true nature as a tool of containment against China. China-US relations are at a crucial stage, as the two sides work to build a "constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness, reciprocity." The consensus reached by the two heads of state must be translated into concrete actions at all levels of government. Washington cannot call for managing differences and stabilizing bilateral ties while allowing exclusive blocs targeting China to pursue increasingly confrontational agendas. Japan's role within the Quad warrants particular vigilance. In recent years, some Japanese political forces have become increasingly keen to use US-led multilateral mechanisms to present their strategic anxieties about China as shared regional concerns. During this meeting, Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi highlighted so-called opposition to "coercion" in the East China Sea and South China Sea. He also raised export restrictions and alleged "overcapacity" during G20 discussions on supply chains. Japan appears to be using collective statements to legitimize its own positions. Such deliberate attempts to tie these issues together not only politicize the Quad's economic security agenda, but also raise further doubts among regional countries about its strategic intentions. India and Australia, meanwhile, each have their own interests and priorities. India emphasizes strategic autonomy and hopes to use multilateral cooperation to create opportunities for industrial development, rather than simply fall in line with an economic containment strategy against China designed by other countries. Australia, for its part, understands that the hard-won stabilization of China-Australia relations in recent years should not be taken for granted. Canberra has little reason to once again place economic and trade cooperation under the shadow of political confrontation just to accommodate the strategic anxieties of certain countries. The differing interests of Quad members make it impossible to forge a united economic front against China through a joint statement alone. In this sense, the Quad could become a hot potato for the US. Since its inception, the grouping has maintained an unmistakably exclusive character, often serving as a platform for containing and pressuring third parties. It has also been used by certain countries to smuggle in their own agendas and turn the grouping into a strategic springboard. This clearly runs counter to regional needs and the broader trend in China-US relations. Washington may hope to use the Quad to coordinate regional resources, but if it allows the grouping to become a megaphone for amplifying disputes with China, it will ultimately have to bear the risks and consequences. Since the US has publicly denied that the Quad is anti-China, it should rein in attempts within the grouping to promote confrontation under the guise of cooperation. Supply chain security matters. But security does not mean exclusion, and resilience does not mean "decoupling." China's position in global manufacturing and critical minerals processing has been built through years of market competition, technological advancement and industrial cooperation. Trying to redraw supply chains by forming exclusive cliques and pursuing bloc politics will not magically create alternative capabilities out of thin air. Instead, it will raise costs for businesses and undermine the region's overall economic vitality and competitiveness. The real test for the Quad is whether it can move beyond the inertia of bloc politics and find areas of cooperation that serve the common interests of the region. Rubio's statement that the Quad is not an "anti-China coalition" could be a positive starting point, but it must not remain mere rhetoric. Washington should value the positive momentum in China-US relations and prevent divisive and confrontational tendencies within regional mechanisms from undermining stability. What the Asia-Pacific needs is cooperation, not division and confrontation.

item.title: South Korea's exports to China surge 133.6% in October amid AI chip boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 22:34:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT South Korea's exports to China surged 133.6 percent year-on-year to $26.98 billion in October, exceeding $20 billion for the fifth consecutive month, the Yonhap News Agency reported on Sunday, citing official data. A Chinese analyst said that the sharp increase, driven largely by semiconductor shipments, highlights the deep integration of the two countries' industrial supply chains amid booming global demand for artificial intelligence (AI). China remained South Korea's largest export destination in October, with shipments reaching $26.98 billion, compared with $24.9 billion to the US. Strong shipments of semiconductors and wireless communications equipment helped drive the growth, according to South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Notably, semiconductor exports to China surged 331 percent year-on-year to $14.8 billion during the first 25 days of October. South Korea's overall exports jumped 93.7 percent year-on-year to $115.3 billion in October, the second-highest monthly total on record, driven by strong semiconductor demand and continued investment in AI infrastructure by major technology companies. Semiconductor exports alone surged 259 percent to $56.4 billion, accounting for nearly half of total shipments, while automobile and cosmetics exports rose 18.1 percent and 57.5 percent, respectively, according to Yonhap. Wang Peng, a Chinese industry analyst, told the Global Times on Sunday that South Korea's export surge reflects a new phase of growth in the global semiconductor industry, driven by expanding AI infrastructure investment and surging demand for memory chips. However, he noted that the growth is concentrated in AI-related chips rather than spread evenly across the industry, making South Korea's export performance increasingly dependent on continued capital spending by major global technology companies. Regarding the sharp increase in exports to China, Wang said that it reflects both strong demand from the Chinese market and the deep integration of the two countries' industrial supply chains. China's expanding AI infrastructure and digital economy have generated substantial demand for semiconductors, while the long-established division of labor between Chinese and South Korean manufacturers has facilitated the movement of intermediate goods and components across their borders, he said. The latest figures also highlight the scale of bilateral economic ties. According to the South Korean Embassy in China, two-way trade reached $263.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026, with South Korean exports to China totaling $145.4 billion. China remained South Korea's largest trading partner, export market and source of imports. Integrated circuits and semiconductor-related components were among South Korea's major exports to China. Wang noted that South Korea's strengths in memory chips complement China's advantages in electronics manufacturing, end-product applications and market scale, making the two economies closely interconnected across the semiconductor value chain. The two countries are no longer simply buyers and sellers, but are deeply embedded in each other's supply chains, he said. The two countries have also been seeking to strengthen economic ties through policy coordination. From October 12 to 16, China and South Korea held the 17th round of negotiations on the second phase of their free trade agreement (FTA) in Seoul, focusing on market access for cross-border services trade and investment under a negative-list approach. Both sides agreed to accelerate the negotiations and work toward their early conclusion, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM). Earlier this year, the MOFCOM said that China and South Korea had signed memorandums of understanding on establishing a bilateral economic and trade cooperation dialogue mechanism and deepening cooperation between industrial parks. The ministry also identified high-end manufacturing, AI and green industries as areas with considerable potential for further cooperation. Wang said that while Chinese and South Korean semiconductor companies face competition in some memory-chip segments, considerable potential remains for cooperation in semiconductor equipment and materials, advanced packaging and AI infrastructure. Emerging sectors such as intelligent vehicles, industrial semiconductors and data centers could offer further opportunities, particularly as the two countries advance their FTA negotiations. Despite adjustments in global supply chains and intensifying technological competition, maintaining stable industrial supply chains and expanding practical cooperation serve the common interests of both countries, he added.

item.title: China-Peru FTA upgrade takes effect, boosting trade efficiency, investment opportunities and regional economic co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 21:12:00
The vessel Xin Shanghai berth at Yangshan Port, Shanghai on December 18, 2024, after a 23-day journey from Chancay Port in Peru. Photo: IC With the upgraded China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) taking effect on Sunday, bilateral trade is expected to become more efficient through streamlined customs procedures and improved supply chain connectivity, creating new opportunities for businesses in both countries and giving fresh impetus to China-Latin America economic cooperation. The upgrade will help Peruvian agricultural products, including blueberries, avocados and grapes, reach Chinese consumers more efficiently, while facilitating Chinese exports of automobiles, machinery and electronics to Peru. Chinese analysts said the agreement could also deepen cooperation in industrial chains, investment and emerging industries. The protocol improves seven existing chapters, including rules of origin, customs procedures, trade facilitation and investment, while adding five new chapters covering standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, electronic commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM). The ministry said the agreement will create a more favorable business environment, expand trade and investment opportunities and bring more tangible benefits to both countries. New opportunities For Peruvian fruit exporters, the upgraded agreement could help address the challenge of getting fresh produce to Chinese buyers with fewer delays and more predictable customs procedures. Gonzalo Matamala, managing director of Southeast Asia and China at INNOF Ltd, a company engaged in fruit trade between China and Latin America, told the Global Times on Sunday that the upgrade's greatest value lies in improving trade efficiency rather than cutting tariffs, as the original agreement already provided substantial benefits. "A container of blueberries, grapes or avocados can lose significant commercial value because of a few days of delays," Matamala said, adding that faster customs clearance and more predictable procedures could directly affect exporters' profitability. According to MOFCOM, the upgraded agreement introduces provisions on electronic networking and detailed arrangements for customs information exchange, cargo clearance, express shipments and perishable goods. It also strengthens transparency and consultation mechanisms concerning sanitary and phytosanitary measures. The new arrangements could complement the logistics advantages brought by Chancay Port, a landmark Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) cooperation project inaugurated in November 2024. The direct shipping route between Chancay and Shanghai has cut transportation time from more than a month to around 23 days, while reducing shipping costs by at least 20 percent, according to a Xinhua News Agency report. In June 2025, Peruvian fruit producer Fruitist shipped its first batch of blueberries for the new season to China through Chancay Port. The shipment arrived in Shanghai about 10 days faster compared to previous transportation arrangements, according to Peru's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In the first 11 months of 2025, the value of fruit imports from Peru through Shanghai ports rose 117.4 percent year-on-year to 2.6 billion yuan ($390.78 million), according to Shanghai customs data cited by local media. Matamala said improved shipping connections and trade procedures could strengthen Peru's competitiveness in China, although the benefits would depend on how effectively customs authorities, shipping companies and exporters implement the new arrangements. Jiang Shixue, distinguished professor from Hangzhou Normal University, also a Chinese expert on Latin American studies, said preferential trade arrangements could give Peruvian products a competitive edge over those from countries without similar agreements. However, he stressed that exporters must first identify market demand to benefit from such arrangements. While improved customs procedures and shipping connections could benefit goods trade, the upgraded agreement also lays the groundwork for closer industrial and investment cooperation. Pan Deng, director of the Latin America and Caribbean Region Law Center at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times that bilateral trade has traditionally centered on resources, agricultural products and manufactured goods, leaving considerable room for closer cooperation in industrial chains and investment. The upgraded agreement provides an institutional foundation for closer cooperation in industrial production, supply chains and investment, Pan said. Improved rules of origin and customs procedures could facilitate trade in intermediate goods, allowing Chinese equipment and technology to support Peru's resource-processing industries and help the country develop local processing capabilities rather than relying mainly on raw material exports. The new global supply chains chapter also encourages multimodal transport and logistics infrastructure development, while improved investment rules and cooperation on standards could reduce barriers to cross-border business, Pan said. The two sides have agreed to launch negative-list negotiations on services and investment within two years of the protocol's entry into force, according to MOFCOM. Wider regional cooperation The upgrade comes as China expands its economic ties with Latin America, where trade and investment links have grown considerably in recent years. China's trade with Latin America reached 3.93 trillion yuan in 2025, up 6.5 percent year-on-year, according to Chinese customs data. China has established FTAs with several Latin American countries, including Chile, Peru, Costa Rica, Ecuador and Nicaragua, according to MOFCOM's free trade agreement network. The latest upgrade with Peru could provide a reference for future efforts to deepen cooperation with other countries in the region. Pan said Chancay Port, combined with the upgraded agreement, could help Chinese businesses expand into other South American markets, including Ecuador, Colombia and Chile. The port's shipping connections, together with improved trade and investment rules, could also encourage companies to establish local processing, warehousing and distribution operations rather than relying solely on exports. Brazil and China were discussing a proposed railway linking Peru's Chancay Port to Brazilian regions, a project that could shorten maritime trade routes to China by at least 10,000 kilometers, Reuters reported in May 2025, citing Brazilian Planning Minister Simone Tebet. Jiang said the China-Peru FTA upgrade could serve as a positive example for broader China-Latin America economic cooperation, expressing hope that more countries in the region would pursue similar arrangements with China. The agreement also comes as rising protectionism and uncertainty over global trade rules pose challenges to international commerce and supply chains. At an APEC trade ministers' meeting in Suzhou in May, participating economies reaffirmed their commitment to advancing regional economic integration, including through the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) agenda, while stressing the importance of resilient supply chains and keeping trade corridors open. The China-Peru FTA upgrade reflects China's efforts to advance trade and investment liberalization through negotiations, offering businesses more predictable rules at a time of growing uncertainty, Chinese experts noted. The Upgrade Protocol also marks a concrete step by China to firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system, and demonstrates China's resolve to work with other countries through free trade negotiations to jointly safeguard multilateralism and free trade, MOFCOM said.

item.title: GT Voice: China's memory chipmakers may lead game of innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 21:11:00
CXMT File photo: VCG China's memory chip industry is moving into new technological territory. Leading memory chipmaker CXMT recently disclosed that it had completed engineering-sample validation of its sixth-generation process technology platform, building upon a key breakthrough in 4F² vertical-channel dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) architecture. The evolution has prompted speculation that CXMT could become the first company in the world to bring 4F²-based products to market, if all goes well. While the outcome remains to be seen, the prospect has already added a new dimension to competition in the global memory arena. Memory chips are used in virtually every modern electronic device that stores data, from smartphones, personal computers and data centers. As artificial intelligence (AI) adoption expands, global demand for memory chips is growing, bringing the industry into greater focus. At the heart of this progress is a new architecture known as 4F². Current mainstream DRAM products use a 6F² cell structure. The 4F² architecture is designed to reduce the area occupied by each memory cell, allowing more data to be stored on a chip of the same size. This makes it an important upgrade to watch in the evolution of next-generation memory technology. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are also exploring such technologies to increase the density of memory integration. According to SBS News, SK Hynix said during a recent earnings call that it plans to develop technologies for a transition to 4F². Yet based on the progress publicly disclosed so far, CXMT appears to be among the global frontrunners in advancing 4F² toward engineering validation. For years, China's memory chip industry has been judged by how quickly it could close the gap with the world's leading players. But that story is beginning to change. While publicly available information is still too limited to make a precise comparison between CXMT's progress on 4F² and that of its international competitors, and the eventual outcome will depend on a range of other factors, CXMT's latest advances offer a glimpse of what is to come. China's memory chip industry is beginning to chart a technological path of its own, rather than follow the course set by established players. Its advances in 4F² suggest that Chinese chipmakers are moving into some of the most advanced areas of next-generation memory research. While the available information offers only a limited basis for assessing how Chinese firms compare technologically with established competitors in South Korea and the US, catching up is no longer the only measure of progress. China's memory chipmakers are moving beyond the task of closing the gap and becoming participants in the competition at the technological frontier of next-generation memory. China's memory chip industry is charting a course with real potential for long-term growth. CXMT reported revenue of 269.02 billion yuan ($40.39 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 738.51 percent year-on-year, and net profit attributable to shareholders of 132.04 billion yuan, reversing a year-earlier loss. The results point to a stronger financial foundation, giving CXMT greater capacity to sustain investment in tech innovations and expand production. CXMT is developing a business model in which commercial returns and technological progress reinforce each other. This offers evidence that China's memory chip industry is on the right path toward building up its competitiveness. The progress of Chinese memory chipmakers could also benefit the global market. As AI drives up demand for memory chips and supplies of some products remain tight, the expansion of China's memory industry will bring additional capacity to the market and give customers more choices. A broader supplier base and stronger competition could help ease supply constraints and make the global memory market more resilient. For China's memory chip industry, the real test is no longer just how quickly it can catch up with established players, but what it can contribute to the next generation of memory technology. The rapid progress in 4F² offers a glimpse of that potential. The next generation innovation needs more participants, not fewer. Broader competition can bring fresh ideas and accelerate technological progress, benefiting the industry as a whole.

item.title: Sultan of Oman makes historic first visit to China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 20:45:00
Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman arrives in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo: Xinhua) Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman arrived in Beijing on Sunday for his two-day state visit to China, media reported, which marks the first visit to China by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established in 1978. Chinese analysts said Oman seeks stronger Chinese engagement amid the evolving situation in the Middle East, and the trip could not only promote cooperation in trade but also set a positive example for regional cooperation. This will be the first visit to China by Sultan Haitham since ascending to the throne and by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established 48 years ago. As such, it is of great significance for advancing bilateral relations, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun introduced during a press conference on Friday. China and Oman enjoy a profound traditional friendship, Guo said. "We hope to work together with the Omani side to take the upcoming visit as an opportunity to bring our strategic partnership to new heights." The visit is expected to strengthen bilateral relations and enhance cooperation between Oman and China across various fields, Times of Oman said in its report on Sunday. The Oman Observer noted that the visit marks a landmark in Omani-Chinese relations. It carries a particular importance in light of the steady evolution of bilateral ties and the wider horizon it holds for deepening the strategic partnership, and it opens the way for closer cooperation across political, economic, investment, cultural and scientific fields, the media outlet said. Sun Degang, director of the Center for Middle Eastern Studies at Fudan University, told the Global Times that the visit to China is to seek stronger Chinese engagement against the backdrop of the evolving situation in the Middle East, as tensions in the Gulf region have escalated sharply recently. Oman hopes that China will play a greater role in actively promoting reconciliation and dialogue, thereby helping to maintain stability in the Middle East, Sun said. Ding Long, a professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University said that Oman's Vision 2040 aims to diversify the economy and reduce its dependence on oil and gas, while China's strengths in renewable energy equipment, infrastructure development, digital technology and industrial supply chains offer the external support Oman needs for its economic transformation. With tensions mounting in the Strait of Hormuz, and Oman, which has been a long-standing active mediator in regional disputes, coming under pressure as well, the visit reflects its efforts to strengthen strategic support and enhance diplomatic autonomy amid great-power rivalry, Ding told the Global Times, adding that the visit could further consolidate China-Oman trade and investment ties. The steady development of relations between China and Oman is an important part of the broader growth of China-Arab cooperation, Sun noted. Since the beginning of this year, China has welcomed a succession of high-level visits from Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The expert added that Sultan Haitham's visit to China further underscores an important point that regardless of the challenges and uncertainties they may face, China's strategic partnerships with Arab countries and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) continue to deepen and deliver tangible results. The visit would have a positive effect across the GCC, Ding added. As one of the few GCC members maintaining communication with the US, Iran and other states, Oman plays a unique role in regional dialogue. Deeper China-Oman ties will help sustain dialogue and inject fresh momentum into China's cooperation with the GCC and the wider Arab world, Sun said.

item.title: Quad's economic coercion claims slammed for double standards
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 19:19:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT The Quad foreign ministers' latest joint statement, which raises concerns over "economic coercion," arbitrary export restrictions and non-market policies without naming China, has drawn criticism from Chinese experts, who questioned the grouping's economic security agenda and warned against turning normal trade and industrial cooperation into instruments of geopolitical competition. Although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed that the Quad is "not an anti-China coalition," the grouping's latest economic rhetoric and expanding focus on supply chains have raised questions about whether its actions match that declaration, analysts said. The statement, released following a meeting of the four foreign ministers in Atlanta on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, reiterates their commitment to building reliable and open global supply chains while criticizing policies and practices that they claimed could disrupt critical industries. Although China was not mentioned in the statement, Reuters reported on Saturday that the statement came as Japan had been highly critical of Beijing's restrictions on critical mineral exports, while Washington had been seeking to rally countries concerned about China's dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals. Asked by Reuters whether the statement's criticism is directed at China, Rubio said the Quad was not established to oppose any particular country. He claimed the Quad was not "an anti-China or anti-anybody coalition," adding that the joint statement is raising concerns about behaviors and activities that he said were "coming repetitively from one country." "If Washington insists that the Quad is not directed against China, then China should not become the unnamed central subject of every meeting," Chen Hong, director of the Institute of Region and Country Studies at East China Normal University, told the Global Times on Sunday. Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Center for American Studies at Fudan University, told the Global Times that although the statement avoids explicitly naming China, its criticism of economic coercion, overcapacity and non-market practices is clearly directed at Beijing. Xin described the rhetoric as a familiar attempt to politicize economic and trade issues and increasingly frame them as matters of national security. Chen said Rubio's remarks could be viewed positively, but Washington needs to demonstrate its intentions through concrete actions. "The nature of the Quad is determined not by how an American official describes it, but by what the grouping actually does," Chen said. Double standards The Quad statement expressed grave concerns over economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity and disrupt critical industries. However, Xin argued that the accusations reflect growing competitive anxiety over China's manufacturing and technological capabilities. China's export controls involving critical minerals have exposed vulnerabilities in some countries' supply chains, while the competitiveness of Chinese manufacturing has intensified pressure on foreign industries, he said. The US has maintained tariffs on Chinese products and restrictions on exports of certain advanced semiconductor technologies to China, citing national security concerns. Washington has also provided substantial government support for domestic semiconductor manufacturing through the CHIPS and Science Act. Xin argued that such policies illustrate the contradictions in Washington's criticism of China's industrial practices. He said the US had pursued semiconductor restrictions, industrial subsidies and efforts to shift production toward preferred partners while accusing China of undermining market rules. Chen similarly questioned what he described as Washington's double standards. "When the US imposes export controls, it calls them measures to safeguard national security. Yet when China implements export controls in accordance with its laws, Washington labels them economic coercion," Chen said. He argued that Washington is attempting to present its protectionist policies as collective economic security initiatives through the Quad. Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times that the Quad's accusations largely repeat familiar rhetoric and lack convincing evidence. Whether the four countries agreed on these claims is less important than whether they reflect economic realities, Zhou said. "Some countries have interfered with global supply chains and undermined their stability, creating additional risks and forcing others to adjust their trade measures," Zhou said. "The question that needs to be clarified is who disrupted these supply chains in the first place." Diverging interests within Quad Despite the common language of the joint statement, the Quad's four members have different economic priorities and relationships with China, according to Chinese experts. The Japanese Foreign Ministry said Saturday's meeting was the third Quad foreign ministers' gathering this year, following meetings in May and July. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi emphasized the importance of demonstrating practical cooperation, particularly in the economic field. The four ministers also discussed regional developments, including the East China Sea and South China Sea, according to the ministry. Chen argued that Japan was increasingly seeking to turn its bilateral concerns about China into a broader multilateral agenda through the Quad. He warned that efforts to promote exclusionary supply chain arrangements could undermine Japan's own economic interests, given its extensive industrial and commercial ties with China. Other Quad members, however, have different calculations. India emphasizes strategic autonomy and seeks opportunities to advance domestic industrial development rather than automatically following Washington's approach, Chen said, adding that Australia also has strong economic incentives to maintain stable relations with China, an important market for its exports. Chen argued that the improvement in China-Australia relations was hard-won and that Canberra had little reason to sacrifice its economic interests to accommodate the strategic concerns of other countries. Rubio's denial of an "anti-China" agenda also reflects Washington's need to accommodate differences among Quad members. For the US, Chen said, the grouping could become a difficult balancing act between coordinating regional partners and maintaining stable relations with China. Supply chain resilience or fragmentation? Beyond its criticism of economic practices, the latest Quad statement outlines several initiatives aimed at strengthening cooperation in critical minerals, semiconductors and emerging technologies. Under the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative Framework announced in May, the four countries pledged to strengthen cooperation on recovering critical minerals from electronic waste and scrap materials. The statement welcomed a US commitment of $10 million to support critical mineral recovery facilities in India and ASEAN countries, while encouraging private investment in processing plants and refineries. The ministers also announced plans to identify potential bottlenecks in semiconductor and advanced computing hardware supply chains before disruptions occur. Additionally, the grouping expressed its intention to provide more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance to support access to trusted artificial intelligence technologies across the so-called "Indo-Pacific." Xin said these initiatives reflect a broader shift in the Quad's agenda from maritime security toward economic, industrial and technological cooperation. He argued that the grouping is increasingly linking supply chain resilience with manufacturing competitiveness and national security, extending geopolitical competition into economic cooperation. However, He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, said Australia possesses significant mineral resources, but developing integrated supply chains requires processing capacity, infrastructure and sustained investment. Xin warned that export controls, technology restrictions and efforts to shift production toward selected partners could further fragment global industrial networks. The consequences, he argued, extended beyond immediate economic costs, potentially weakening countries' confidence in the stability of international economic arrangements. Chen stressed that efforts to stabilize China-US relations required consistent policies across different areas of Washington's foreign policy, including implementation of understandings reached between the two countries' leaders. "If the Quad wants to demonstrate its value, it should prove that it can deliver genuine public goods to the region, rather than relying on the creation of a common adversary to maintain internal cohesion," Chen said.

item.title: Africa's Olympic debut, with China-Africa cooperation setting the stage
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 17:22:00
The Olympic rings are displayed during the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal on October 31, 2026. Photo: Xinhua On October 31, the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games opened, marking the first time the African continent has hosted an Olympic sporting event. International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said, "This historic moment is for Senegal, for Africa." The flame is lit, and the venues are buzzing. The cameras focus on the athletes and the stands - the rightful protagonists of event coverage. But a historic sporting event is not only about the cheers in front of the scenes; it also depends on the support behind them. Its real significance lies in the foundation that makes the event possible. According to public information, China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) undertook the renovation and expansion of Iba Mar Diop Stadium, one of the main venues of the Youth Olympic Games, including an 8,000-seat football stadium, an international-standard athletics track, an indoor handball hall, a multipurpose gymnasium and other supporting facilities. In this sense, Africa's Olympic "debut" stands on a venue built through joint China-Africa cooperation. What sustains a historic moment? A major sporting event is never just a competition lasting a dozen days; it is also a concentrated test of urban infrastructure. Venues, tracks, lighting and stands - things that never mount the podium - determine whether a continent can firmly host its "first." This is the core issue behind Africa's Olympic debut. China's role here is not to host the Games on Africa's behalf, but to participate as a partner in setting the stage. The stage belongs to Senegal and to Africa; the builders are partners standing side by side. This relationship matters. China-Africa cooperation has been discussed for many years, and the most visible examples are railways, ports and highways. Sports venues follow the same logic: They turn development aspirations into tangible public goods. For local young people, a standard running track or a stadium capable of hosting international events may be more concrete than any grand narrative. Building the venues is only the first step. More important is what comes after the Games: How they will be operated, how they will benefit communities and how construction-period jobs can become long-term capacity. After the Youth Olympic Games, the venues will continue to open to local athletes and young people, helping drive sports training and the event economy, and turning "built by China" from hardware into real development dividends. That is where China-Africa cooperation should focus on more in the next stage: not only "turnkey delivery," but also "leaving capacity"; not only building a venue, but also driving development in the surrounding area. The policy principle of sincerity, real results, amity and good faith toward Africa must ultimately translate into concrete projects and tangible, accessible gains for local people. That is the lasting measure of this cooperation. Africa's first hosting of an Olympic sporting event is a coming-of-age ceremony for the continent. China's construction presence appears at the sidelines: It need not steal the spotlight, nor should it be overlooked. It reminds us that a historic moment needs the flame, but also a foundation; it needs applause, but also someone to build the stands solidly. The central point is simple: this debut rests on shared effort. The stage is Africa's; the cooperation is shared. From the Railway to the Olympic venues, the forms of China-Africa cooperation are changing. Still, the logic of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits remains unchanged. The opening of a sporting event reflects the steady, step-by-step progress of China and Africa pursuing modernization together. It serves as a quiet footnote to the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity.

item.title: Hong Kong police, corporate partners team up anti-scam livestreams for mainland students
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 17:15:00
Photo: Screenshot from Xiaohongshu The Anti-Deception Coordination Centre (ADCC) of the Hong Kong Police Force (HKPF), China Mobile Hong Kong's s/ash brand and Chinese lifestyle-focused social media platform Xiaohongshu last Wednesday jointly held their first online anti-scam livestream for mainland students planning to study or already studying in the Hong Kong amid a rise in scams targeting the group, Hong Kong local media outlets reported. Preoccupied with matters such as visas and academic studies, newly arrived mainland students in Hong Kong are particularly vulnerable to scams due to their unfamiliarity with local systems and channels for seeking assistance and limited access to reliable information. The main types of fraud targeting these students include phone, rental, job and romance-investment scams, as well as "virtual kidnapping" scams targeting their families, local media outlet HK01 reported. According to statistics from the ADCC, Hong Kong recorded 512 scam cases involving mainland students in the first eight months of 2026, resulting in losses of HK$110 million ($14.02 million). University students, particularly Chinese mainland students in their first year of study in Hong Kong, are increasingly targeted by scams involving impostors posing as government officials or customer service representatives, police said. A PhD student was defrauded of HK$5 million in an impersonation scam after fraudsters posing as immigration department officers tricked the victim into downloading the Microsoft Teams app, signing a confidentiality agreement, agreeing to round-the-clock surveillance and borrowing money from family members under the pretext of funding an exchange program in the US, according to HK01. Zhang Ting, a Shanghai resident whose son is a freshman at the University of Hong Kong, told the Global Times on Sunday that all her family members have received scam phone calls since her son's enrollment at the university. The scammers posing as Hong Kong immigration officers contact them under the pretext of issuing summonses or penalty notices. Zhang thinks anti-scam campaigns organized by the Hong Kong police and the educational institutions are essential and very helpful to mainland students. She and her family will continue to follow such campaigns, particularly those highlighting emerging scams involving AI technology. During the livestream, an ADCC official outlined common and AI-powered scams through real-life cases, urging students to follow the "hang up, verify, seek help" advice and use official resources, including the Scameter app and anti-scam helpline, to better protect themselves. The initiative moves beyond traditional anti-scam awareness campaigns by bringing police and corporate partners together. Drawing on social media platforms popular among mainland students and business partners' networks, it aims to make anti-scam education more engaging through formats young people famor, including livestreams, interactive Q&A sessions and real-life case studies, Hong Kong-based Bauhinia Magazine reported. The organizers said the anti-scam class was the first initiative in a broader campaign, which will later be expanded to university and college campuses. Plans include an upcoming territory-wide "Dem Beat anti-scam competition" with the aim of continuously raising awareness of scam prevention among non-local students studying in Hong Kong, according to HK01.

item.title: More than 800 people honored for reporting activities endangering national security as hotline marks 11th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-01 15:38:00
Photo: China's Ministry of State Security More than 800 people have been commended and rewarded for reporting activities endangering China's national security since 2019, as the national security authorities' 12339 public hotline marks its 11th anniversary this year, according to an article published on the official WeChat account of China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) on Sunday. The hotline, officially launched in November 2015, serves as a channel connecting the public with national security authorities, enabling citizens and organizations to report suspected activities that threaten national security through telephone calls and online platforms. Over the past 11 years, the number of reports received through the hotline has continued to rise, with an increasing number of high-quality leads emerging and contributing to the investigation of multiple major cases, the article said. Since 2019, national security authorities have organized nationwide commendation and reward programs for individuals who have made meritorious contributions through reporting in accordance with the Counter-Espionage Law as well as other laws and regulations. More than 800 people have received recognition and rewards over the past eight years, according to the article. In 2022, MSS released the regulation on rewards for citizens reporting activities that endanger national security who will be given an incentive based on the effectiveness and contribution of their reports, with the maximum amount exceeding 100,000 yuan ($15,000). The MSS article published on Sunday also highlighted several examples of citizens who helped safeguard national security by reporting suspicious activities. They included border residents who stepped forward to confront and thwart suspicious individuals and received awards for particularly significant contributions; a ride-hailing driver who noticed a passenger secretly photographing a sensitive facility and calmly handled the situation; fishermen who retrieved surveillance devices from the sea; and a university student who reported the sale of state secrets. The article said that China's counter-espionage efforts face a severe and complex situation, with foreign intelligence agencies seeking to infiltrate the country and obtain sensitive information. It stressed that safeguarding national security requires not only the efforts of national security authorities but also the participation of the public. The experience of the past 11 years demonstrates that safeguarding national security is a responsibility shared by all, with growing public participation helping strengthen the country's overall national security defenses, it added. Global Times

item.title: Chinese tech firm gives employees gold keyboard keycaps for fifth straight year
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 14:05:00
A tech company in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, gave 20 gold keyboard keycaps to outstanding employees as gifts for Programmers' Day in China on October 24. Photos: Jimu News A tech company in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, gave 20 gold keyboard keycaps to outstanding employees as gifts for Programmers' Day in China on October 24. One of the keycaps, a gold space bar weighing about 35 grams, is worth more than 40,000 yuan ($6,000), Jimu News reported. The company, Insta360, an intelligent imaging technology firm, has presented gold keycaps to outstanding employees for five consecutive years, giving away a total of 75, according to the media report. Nearly 60 percent of its workforce is engaged in research and development (R&D), with R&D personnel playing a key role in driving product innovation. Each year, the largest gold space bar is awarded to the programmer who has made the greatest contribution to the company. This year, the company also introduced gold "F5" keys, symbolizing iterative improvement and innovation. Each F5 key is worth nearly 10,000 yuan, while all the keycaps are made of approximately 99.9 percent pure gold. With gold prices fluctuating, the gold keycaps have unexpectedly become a kind of "investment product" in employees' eyes, although many choose to keep them as souvenirs. In a post on his Sina Weibo account recently, Insta360 CEO Liu Jingkang said that a young colleague had suggested giving this year's gold keycaps to artificial intelligence (AI) instead of employees, but he disagreed. While AI has made it possible to generate code in ever-greater quantities, the value that exceptional people can create has actually become even greater, Liu said. As more code is generated by AI, the company still chooses to reward human creativity with real gold, he added. Global Times
